# Draft:Palestinian Resistance to Colonialism

The First intifada
Since the occupation of the West Bank and the Gaza Strip in the Six-Day War of 1967, the twenty-year occupation brought little to no improvement in the material conditions of Palestinian lives, with settler violence worsening (Said, 1989, p. 24). Palestinians continued to pay taxes without representation and required permits for planting trees, digging wells, and entering or exiting the territories, while raising the Palestinian flag remained punishable by jail time (Said, 1989, p. 24).
According to Naser-Najjab (2020), the first Intifada was a widespread Palestinian uprising within the West Bank and Gaza Strip (p. 62). The igniting factor was in December 1987 when an Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) truck crashed into and killed four Palestinians in Jabalia Camp, located in northern Gaza (Naser-Najjab, 2020, p. 62). This event led to a large-scale, bottom-up uprising, characterized primarily by peaceful forms of resistance (Naser-Najjab, 2020, p. 62). These forms of resistance mainly consisted of popular protests, strikes, and the establishment of alternative educational institutions .
One example of grassroots resistance to the occupation took place in the small Christian town of Beit Sahour, south of Jerusalem. As part of a boycott movement in 1988, residents decided to stop buying Israeli milk and instead established their own dairy farm. The Israeli government promptly shut the farm down, claiming that "these cows are dangerous for the security of the State of Israel” (The First Intifada — Dutch Scholars for Palestine, 2025). The following year, Palestinian residents refused to pay taxes to the Israeli government, adopting the slogan “No taxation without representation.” In response, the Israeli army raided the town and demolished the homes of Palestinians who refused to comply. As an act of defiance, residents threw away their Israeli-issued identity cards, which they were legally mandated to carry.
Another example of resistance during the first Intifada occurred at Birzeit University. A common tactic of repression by the Israeli government was the banning of thousands of books and the deportation of teachers and students (Said, 1989, p. 24). This was followed by the closure of Birzeit University for 51 months. In response, secret classes were held in rooms facilitated by the Young Women’s and Men’s Christian Associations (YWCA and YMCA) (The First Intifada — Dutch Scholars for Palestine, 2025).
